chapter.name: Constructions and Tilings
chapter.blurb: Ruler and compass constructions of the perpendicular bisector, 90, 45, 60 and 30 degree angles, angle copying, parallel lines, the regular hexagon and star, and tiling regions and the plane.

scope: Explain bisection and the perpendicular bisector, and justify through congruence that a point at equal distance from the ends of a segment lies on its perpendicular bisector
Construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment and a 90 degree angle at a point on a line with an unmarked ruler and compass, and the rope method of the Sulba-Sutras
Bisect an angle and copy an angle using the SSS congruence condition, and construct 45 degree and eight-petalled designs
Construct a line parallel to a given line by copying a corresponding angle, and a perpendicular from a point outside a line
Use angles around a point (360 degrees) to build a regular hexagon from six equilateral triangles, construct 60, 120, 30 and 15 degree angles and the six-pointed star
Decide whether a region can be tiled with 2 x 1 tiles using counting and black-and-white colouring
Tile the entire plane with squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons, and know that other shapes and mixed shapes can also tile it
Constructing a regular pentagon -- the chapter defers it to later classes
Constructing an angle of an exact given measure such as 65.5 degrees -- only a Math Talk question and not developed
Tangram rearrangement puzzles and the optical illusion figure -- recreational and not assessed
Proving which polygons can tile the plane in general -- the chapter only shows examples

concepts.name: Perpendicular bisector and points equidistant from two points
concepts.description: Understanding bisection and the perpendicular bisector and proving through congruent triangles that points at equal distance from the ends of a segment lie on its perpendicular bisector.
concepts.idea: Two points that are each at equal distance from X and Y give congruent triangles, so the line through them cuts XY in half at a right angle.
concepts.rule: Any point at equal distance from X and Y lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY, and the perpendicular bisector is the only such line.
concepts.example: If AX = AY = BX = BY then triangle ABX is congruent to triangle ABY by SSS and AB bisects XY at right angles.

concepts.name: Constructing the perpendicular bisector and a 90 degree angle
concepts.description: Constructing the perpendicular bisector of a segment and a 90 degree angle at a point on a line using an unmarked ruler and compass, and the rope method.
concepts.idea: Arcs of equal radius from the two ends locate points equidistant from both ends, and two such points fix the perpendicular bisector.
concepts.rule: Use the same radius from X and from Y for each pair of arcs; for a 90 degree angle at O first mark X and Y at equal distance from O so that O is the midpoint.
concepts.example: The midpoint of a rope stretched between pegs at X and Y is equidistant from both, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector.

concepts.name: Bisecting and copying angles
concepts.description: Bisecting an angle and copying an angle with a ruler and compass, justified by the SSS congruence condition, and using bisection to get 45 degree angles.
concepts.idea: Equal arcs make triangles with three pairs of equal sides, so their corresponding angles are equal.
concepts.rule: To bisect angle XOY mark OA = OB and draw equal arcs from A and B meeting at C; OC bisects the angle. To copy an angle, copy an isosceles triangle by SSS.
concepts.example: Bisecting a 90 degree angle gives 45 degrees, and 360 degrees divided into 8 equal parts gives 45 degrees.

concepts.name: Constructing parallel and perpendicular lines
concepts.description: Constructing a line parallel to a given line by copying a corresponding angle, and a perpendicular from a point outside a line.
concepts.idea: Equal corresponding angles on a transversal give parallel lines, and a point equidistant from two points of a line lies on their perpendicular bisector.
concepts.rule: Copy the angle between the given line and a transversal at the new point; for a perpendicular from P, cut the line at X and Y with PX = PY and bisect XY.
concepts.example: Copying a 65 degree angle at B on the transversal gives a line through B parallel to the given line.

concepts.name: Angles at a point, 60 degrees and the regular hexagon
concepts.description: Using the fact that angles around a point add up to 360 degrees, constructing 60, 120, 30 and 15 degree angles, the regular hexagon and the six-pointed star.
concepts.idea: An equilateral triangle gives a 60 degree angle, and six of them fit exactly around a point to form a regular hexagon.
concepts.rule: Angles around a point add to 360 degrees; six equilateral triangles fill it; a regular hexagon has angles of 120 degrees and its centre is at distance equal to its side from every vertex.
concepts.example: The angles 40, 60, 50, 30, 40 and 90 degrees leave a gap of 50 degrees, so a 70 degree angle does not fit.

concepts.name: Tiling regions with 2 x 1 tiles
concepts.description: Deciding whether a region can be tiled with 2 x 1 tiles by counting squares and by black-and-white colouring.
concepts.idea: Each tile covers exactly two squares, one of each colour in a chessboard colouring, so the counts of squares must match.
concepts.rule: A region with an odd number of squares cannot be tiled; a tileable region has equal numbers of black and white squares; a grid with one even side can be tiled.
concepts.example: A 5 x 7 grid has 35 squares so it cannot be tiled, and a 4 x 6 grid needs 12 tiles.

concepts.name: Tiling the plane
concepts.description: Tiling the entire plane with squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons, using the angles around a point, and recognising that mixed and irregular shapes can tile too.
concepts.idea: Shapes tile the plane when the angles that meet at each point add up to 360 degrees with no gap or overlap.
concepts.rule: Squares (4 x 90), equilateral triangles (6 x 60) and regular hexagons (3 x 120) each tile the plane; combinations tile if their angles add to 360 degrees.
concepts.example: Two hexagons and two triangles meet at a point with 120 + 120 + 60 + 60 = 360 degrees.
